summary: Defines Opaque LSAs for OSPF, a generalized way to carry application-specific information using standard flooding, so OSPF can be extended later. It adds a mechanism for validating AS-scope Opaque LSAs originated outside a router's area. It replaces RFC 2370. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF carries information in advertisements called LSAs. This document gives it three more kinds whose contents are left to other applications, so that new information can travel through an OSPF network without anyone changing OSPF. Each kind has a rule about how far it may travel.

subtitle: A generic container for OSPF to flood extra, application-specific data with the normal link-state machinery.

tldr.problem: Every new piece of information OSPF might want to carry needs a new LSA type, and each new type changes the protocol that all routers must agree on.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines three new LSA types, 9, 10 and 11, that carry a standard LSA header followed by application-specific data. Each type has a flooding scope: link-local, area-local or the whole autonomous system.
tldr.outcome: Applications can distribute information through an OSPF domain without changing OSPF itself, and the scope rules keep a link-local advertisement from escaping its link. The document replaced RFC 2370 in 2008 and added a way to check the originator of a domain-wide Opaque LSA.

today: RFC 5250 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 2370 in 2008, adding the mechanism for validating AS-scope Opaque LSAs originated outside the router's area, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It extends OSPF itself, defined in RFC 2328.

sections.title: Why Opaque LSAs
sections.content:
OSPF has been widely deployed throughout the Internet, and as deployment and networking technology have evolved, OSPF has been extended to support many options. That evolution will continue.

This document defines enhancements to OSPF to support a new class of link state advertisements called Opaque LSAs, which provide a generalized mechanism for the future extensibility of OSPF. The information they carry may be used directly by OSPF or indirectly by some application that wants to distribute information throughout the OSPF domain. The exact use of Opaque LSAs is beyond the scope of the document.

An Opaque LSA consists of a standard LSA header followed by a 32-bit aligned application-specific information field. Like any other LSA, it uses the link-state database distribution mechanism for flooding, so the information travels by ordinary OSPF rules. The link-state type field identifies the range of topological distribution, which is called the flooding scope.

The document expects an implementation of the option to provide an application interface for three things: encapsulating application-specific information in a specific Opaque type, sending and receiving that information, and telling the application when previously received information has become invalid because of a topological change.
sections.plainLanguage: The point is to stop changing the routing protocol every time someone wants to send new information through it. The advertisement carries whatever the application wants, and OSPF only moves it around and keeps it within its allowed range.

sections.title: The Three Types and Their Scopes
sections.content:
Opaque LSAs are link state advertisements of types 9, 10 and 11. The link-state type identifies the flooding scope. A value of 9 denotes a link-local scope, and type-9 LSAs are not flooded beyond the local (sub)network. A value of 10 denotes an area-local scope, and type-10 LSAs are not flooded beyond the borders of their associated area. A value of 11 means the LSA is flooded throughout the Autonomous System, with a scope equivalent to that of AS-External (type-5) LSAs: flooded throughout all transit areas, not flooded into stub areas or Not-So-Stubby Areas from the backbone, and not originated by routers into their connected stub areas or NSSAs. As with type-5 LSAs, a type-11 Opaque LSA received in a stub area or NSSA from a neighbour inside that area is rejected.

The link-state ID of an Opaque LSA is divided into an Opaque Type field, the first 8 bits, and a type-specific ID in the remaining 24 bits. The opaque information field holds some number of octets of application data, padded to 32-bit alignment.

The responsibility for honouring the scope lies with both the sender and the receiver. The receiver must always store a valid received Opaque LSA in its link-state database, and must not accept one that violates its flooding scope.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds, and the kind decides how far the advertisement travels: to the local link only, to the local area only, or across the whole network. The receiver checks the rule and drops anything that breaks it.

sections.title: The Opaque LSA Packet Format
sections.content:
The packet format has the same header as any other LSA: an LS age, an Options field and the link-state type, which holds 9, 10 or 11. The link-state ID is split between the Opaque Type and the Opaque ID. The rest of the header carries the advertising router, the LS sequence number, the LS checksum and the length. After that comes the Opaque Information field, which holds the application-specific octets padded to 32-bit alignment.

The Options field is present in Hello packets, Database Description packets and all link state advertisements. It lets a router say which optional capabilities it supports, so routers of differing capabilities can be mixed in one routing domain. In Hello packets it lets a router reject a neighbour because of a capability mismatch; in Database Description packets it lets a router choose not to flood certain advertisements to that neighbour; and in link state advertisements it lets routers steer traffic around a router with reduced functionality. All eight bits have been assigned, although only the O-bit is described fully by this document. Routers should clear unrecognised bits when sending, and should ignore an unrecognised capability and process the packet normally when receiving one.
sections.plainLanguage: The advertisement reuses the standard OSPF header and adds a payload for the application. The options byte in that header is how routers say which of these new advertisements they understand.

sections.title: Flooding Opaque LSAs and the Summary List
sections.content:
The flooding of Opaque LSAs must follow the scope rules, and the ordinary OSPF flooding procedure applies otherwise, with the modifications given here. If the LSA is type-9 and the interface it was received on is not the same as the target interface, it must be discarded and not acknowledged, and an implementation should keep track of the IP interface associated with each link-local Opaque LSA. If the LSA is type-10 and the area it belongs to is not the same as the area of the target interface, it must likewise be discarded and not acknowledged, and the area should be tracked for each area-local Opaque LSA. If the LSA is type-11 and the target interface belongs to a stub area or NSSA, it must not be flooded out of that interface, and one received on such an interface must be discarded and not acknowledged, because the neighbouring router flooded it in error.

When opaque-capable and non-opaque-capable routers are mixed in one domain, Opaque LSAs are typically not flooded to the routers that cannot read them. As a general design principle, optional OSPF advertisements are only flooded to routers that understand them. A router learns of its neighbour's capability at the start of the Database Exchange process: a neighbour is opaque-capable if and only if it sets the O-bit in the Options field of its Database Description packets. The O-bit should not be set, and must be ignored, in packets other than Database Description packets. When flooding, Opaque LSAs must be placed on the retransmission lists of opaque-capable neighbours and must not be placed on the lists of non-opaque-capable neighbours, though a non-opaque-capable router may still receive one in a multicast Link State Update and will simply discard it.

Information contained in received Opaque LSAs should only be used when the router that originated the LSA is reachable. Reachability validation may be done less frequently than every SPF calculation, and a router processing received Opaque LSAs may choose to give priority to the base OSPF LSA types.

The OSPF neighbour state machine is unchanged except for one action, the one that builds the Database summary list during the ExStart state on the NegotiationDone event. The router must list the contents of its entire area link-state database in the neighbour's summary list: the Router LSAs, Network LSAs, Summary LSAs, type-9 and type-10 Opaque LSAs in the area structure, together with the AS External and type-11 Opaque LSAs in the global structure.

Some things are left out. AS External and type-11 Opaque LSAs must be omitted from a virtual neighbour's summary list, and must also be omitted if the area is configured as a stub area or NSSA. Type-9 Opaque LSAs must be omitted if the interface associated with the neighbour is not the interface the Opaque LSA came in on. Any advertisement whose age equals MaxAge must be omitted and instead added to the neighbour's link-state retransmission list. A summary of the list is sent to the neighbour in Database Description packets, of which only one may be outstanding at a time.
sections.plainLanguage: Before an advertisement is forwarded, the router checks that it stays within its allowed range and that the neighbour on the other side understands this kind of advertisement at all. When two routers first meet, the list they exchange also has rules: some of these advertisements are left out because of where they may travel.

sections.title: Checking the Originator of a Domain-Wide LSA
sections.content:
Type-11 Opaque LSAs are flooded throughout the Autonomous System, and that raises one problem: routers in remote areas need a way to check that the router which originated the LSA is still available. If a router originates a type-11 LSA and then goes out of service, routers outside its area have no way of detecting that and may use the stale information for a considerable period, up to 60 minutes. Type-9 and type-10 LSAs do not have this problem, because a receiving router can detect whether the advertising router is reachable within the LSA's own flooding scope: for type-9 the originating router must be an OSPF neighbour in Exchange state or greater, and for type-10 the intra-area SPF calculation determines reachability.

OSPF already has an answer for the same problem with type-5 LSAs: AS border router information advertised in type-4 Summary LSAs. This document reuses that mechanism for type-11 Opaque LSAs. A router configured to originate AS-scope Opaque LSAs advertises itself as an ASBR and must follow the requirements for the Options field E-bit in OSPF LSA headers. Routers can then track the originator's reachability directly through the SPF calculation, for routers in the same area, or indirectly through the type-4 LSAs originated by area border routers, for routers in other areas. The solution does not apply to stub areas or NSSAs, because AS-scoped Opaque LSAs are not flooded into those area types.

When processing a received type-11 Opaque LSA, the router must look up the routing table entries for the ASBR that originated it. If there are no entries, the ASBR is unreachable, and the router must do nothing with the LSA. It must also stop using all the Opaque LSAs injected by that same originator once the originator is detected to be unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: A router outside the area cannot tell whether the router that sent an advertisement has died, so it might act on old information. The fix is the same one OSPF already uses for external routes: the originator announces itself as a border router so everyone can check whether it is still there.

sections.title: Management and Compatibility
sections.content:
The updated OSPF MIB, RFC 4750, provides explicit support for Opaque LSAs and should be used to support implementations of this document. Implementations that support it also include Opaque LSAs in the appropriate generic LSA objects, for example ospfOriginateNewLsas and ospfLsdbTable.

Backward compatibility is straightforward. A non-opaque-capable neighbour that receives an Opaque LSA simply discards it, as OSPF already requires for LSAs of unknown type. The one caveat the document notes is that OSPF routers that implement the earlier version of this option will keep using stale type-11 LSAs even when the originator implements the inter-area procedures described above, because those routers do not know to check.
sections.plainLanguage: Old routers that do not know about these advertisements simply throw them away, so nothing breaks. The only cost is that an old router will not notice when the originator of a domain-wide advertisement dies.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two kinds of issue need addressing when protecting routing protocols from misconfiguration and malicious attack. The first is authentication and certification of routing protocol information. The second is denial-of-service attacks from repetitive origination of the same advertisement, or from originating a large number of distinct advertisements, which overflows the database. Both concerns exist independently of a router's support for the Opaque option.

For authentication, OSPF exchanges are authenticated, with the type of authentication configured per network segment. The cryptographic authentication option appends a message digest to each transmitted packet, and receivers use the shared secret key and the received digest to verify that the packet is authentic. The quality of that protection depends on the strength of the message digest algorithm, MD5 being the only one specified at the time, the strength of the key, correct implementation everywhere, and the secrecy of the shared key. None of the standard OSPF authentication types provide confidentiality, and none protect against traffic analysis.

For the denial-of-service concerns, OSPF limits how often a new instance of any particular LSA may be originated, to once every MinLSInterval seconds, whose value is 5, and how often new instances may be accepted during flooding, to once every MinLSArrival seconds, whose value is 1. Database overflow, when the link-state database becomes too large for some routers, can be handled by configuring stub areas and NSSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: The document repeats OSPF's own security rules: authenticate the packets, and limit how often the same advertisement can be sent so nobody can flood the network with them.

sections.title: The Opaque Type Registry
sections.content:
The document updates the requirements for the OSPF Opaque LSA type registry with three changes. References to the earlier version of this option are replaced with references to this document. The Opaque type values in the range 128 to 255 are reserved for private use. And the reference for registry value 1, the Traffic Engineering LSA, is updated to RFC 3630.

The registry has two ranges: 0 to 127 allocated by IETF consensus, and 128 to 255 for private use. Within it, value 1 is the Traffic Engineering LSA, value 2 is Sycamore Optical Topology Descriptions, value 3 is the grace-LSA, value 4 is Router Information (RI), values 5 to 127 are unassigned, and values 128 to 255 are private use.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of Opaque LSA carries an 8-bit type number that says what the payload is. The numbers up to 127 are handed out by the IETF; 128 to 255 are for private use.

cells: Not flooded beyond the borders of their associated area.

viz.caption: THE OPAQUE LSA HEADER (RFC 5250 APPENDIX A.2)

fields.name: Options
fields.desc: The capabilities of the router that originated the LSA.

fields.name: Link-State Type
fields.desc: 9, 10 or 11. The type sets the flooding scope.

fields.name: Opaque Type
fields.desc: The first 8 bits of the link-state ID: what the application-specific information is.

fields.name: Opaque ID
fields.desc: The remaining 24 bits of the link-state ID: the type-specific identifier.

fields.name: Advertising Router
fields.desc: The router that originated the LSA.

fields.name: LS Sequence Number
fields.desc: Increments for each new instance of the LSA.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the LSA in bytes.

viz.caption: THE OSPF OPTIONS FIELD (RFC 5250 APPENDIX A.1)

fields.name: DN
fields.desc: Used to prevent looping in BGP/MPLS IP VPNs.

fields.name: O
fields.desc: The router is willing to receive and forward Opaque LSAs. This is the bit that marks a neighbour as opaque-capable.

fields.name: DC
fields.desc: The router's handling of demand circuits.

fields.name: EA
fields.desc: The router is willing to receive and forward External-Attributes-LSAs.

fields.name: N/P
fields.desc: The router's handling of type-7 LSAs.

fields.name: MC
fields.desc: Whether IP multicast datagrams are forwarded as specified.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: The way AS-External LSAs are flooded.
